wine.name: Vin de Constance
wine.grapes: Muscat de Frontignan alone, the Cape's name for Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains.
wine.sites: The estate's own vineyards on the slopes of the Constantiaberg, on decomposed granite, cooled by sea breezes from the Atlantic and from False Bay.
wine.making: The bunches are left to shrivel on the vine and picked by hand in many passes, from fresh, high acid berries to raisins, each batch kept apart. Most batches spend about two weeks on their skins before pressing. No spirit is added. By the house's recent sheets the wine is aged about eighteen months in 500 litre oak barrels, about half new of French, Hungarian and Austrian oak, then for well over a year more in large foudres.
wine.glass: Candied orange peel, dried apricot, barley sugar and black tea over honey; sweet and rich, yet kept fresh by bright acidity rather than spirit, with a long, clean finish.
wine.ageing: Open and generous on release, its sugar and acidity carry it for decades in a cool cellar, where it gathers notes of tea and dried fruit.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a small white wine glass and a modest pour.

records.table: Vin de Constance is Klein Constantia's revival of the sweet wine of old Constantia: Muscat de Frontignan shrivelled on the vine, never fortified, and aged long in oak. It tastes of candied orange peel, apricot and black tea, so pour it cool and in small glasses.
records.story: In 1685 Simon van der Stel (1639 to 1712), the Dutch East India Company's commander and later governor at the Cape, was granted land on the slopes of the Constantiaberg. After his death in 1712 the estate was divided, and Klein Constantia, Little Constantia, took shape later as a portion split from it early in the nineteenth century. Through the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries the sweet wine of Constantia crossed to Europe: Napoleon Bonaparte (1769 to 1821) had it shipped to his exile on St Helena, and in Sense and Sensibility by Jane Austen (1775 to 1817), published in 1811, Mrs Jennings offers a glass of old Constantia for a broken heart. The trade faded from the 1860s, when Britain removed the preference its tariffs had given Cape wine, and phylloxera then ruined the vineyards late in the century, so the wine ceased to be made. In 1980, by most accounts, a new owner bought and replanted the run down farm, with Muscat de Frontignan set aside to bring the old wine back. The 1986 vintage, two barrels of it, was the first Vin de Constance of the revival, bottled in a 500 millilitre bottle designed in Italy after the antique. The family sold the estate in 2011. It carries the Cape's eighteenth century story into the glass, sweet with no spirit at all.

wine.name: Grand Constance
wine.grapes: Red and white Muscat de Frontignan, the two colours of Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains, as in the estate's historic wine.
wine.sites: By the house's account, a block of Muscat de Frontignan beside the Manor House, on the slopes below the Constantiaberg.
wine.making: The grapes are left late on the vine to shrivel, without noble rot, and picked as raisined berries. They ferment on their skins for about a week before pressing. The wine is not fortified, and it then returns to barrel: about two years by the house's recent sheets, eighteen months in old French oak by an earlier page.
wine.glass: Amber in the glass, with dried apricot, orange zest, honey and caramel over Turkish delight and rose petal; sweet and creamy, with a hint of bitter almond on the finish.
wine.ageing: Ready on release, it has the sugar and acidity to keep and deepen for many years, turning towards toffee and dried fruit.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a small white wine glass and a modest pour.

records.table: Grand Constance is Groot Constantia's own revival of the sweet wine that made the farm famous: red and white Muscat de Frontignan shrivelled on the vine beside the Manor House, unfortified and aged in barrel. Amber, it tastes of apricot, honey and rose petal.
records.story: Groot Constantia is the heart of the land granted in 1685 to Simon van der Stel (1639 to 1712), commander and then governor of the Cape for the Dutch East India Company, and it keeps his manor house. After his death the estate was broken up and sold in parts. In December 1778 by the house's account, 1779 by others, the farm passed to Hendrik Cloete (1725 to 1799), who planted vineyards, enlarged the house and in 1791 added a wine cellar. Under the Cloete family the red and white Muscat wines of Constantia were sold to Europe's courts and tables. The family kept the farm until 1885, when it fell insolvent and the state took it on. Fire gutted the manor house in December 1925, and it was restored in the Cape Dutch style from 1926; in 1969 the house became part of the South African Cultural History Museum. In 1993 the estate passed to the Groot Constantia Trust. A decade later, with the 2003 vintage, the cellar began to make Grand Constance again from Muscat de Frontignan grown beside the Manor House, more than a century after the old wine had ceased. It is the sweet wine of the farm that first made Constantia's name, made again where the old one was made.

wine.name: Magna Carta
wine.grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, the larger part, from about three fifths to seven tenths in the vintages read, with Sémillon for the rest.
wine.sites: The estate's own vineyards in southern Constantia, on Clovelly, Oakleaf and Avalon soils; the Sauvignon Blanc of the first vintage came from the house's Reserve block.
wine.making: The two grapes are made apart. The Sémillon is left to hang late for full ripeness and its clean juice is fermented in 500 and 600 litre French oak barrels in the later vintages read; in the first vintage the Sauvignon Blanc saw no oak. After blending the wine goes back to barrels of various ages for some months before bottling, and it is made only in years the house judges strong enough.
wine.glass: Elderflower, jasmine and star anise over quince preserve, marmalade and vanilla pod; smooth and weighty from the Sémillon, lifted by the freshness of the Sauvignon Blanc.
wine.ageing: Tight when it is young, it has the Sémillon and the oak to build texture in bottle for some years after release.
wine.serve: 10 to 13 degrees Celsius; no need to decant, though a young bottle opens with air; a white Burgundy glass.

records.table: Magna Carta is Steenberg's white blend from southern Constantia: Sauvignon Blanc for freshness and barrel fermented Sémillon for weight, made only in strong years. It smells of elderflower, jasmine and quince, so serve it cool rather than cold in a wide glass.
records.story: Steenberg dates itself to 1682, when, by the house's account, Simon van der Stel (1639 to 1712), commander of the Cape, leased land at the foot of the mountain to a settler from Lübeck, Catharina Ras, whom the house counts as the first woman to hold land under the Dutch East India Company at the Cape. The farm's first name was Swaaneweide, the swans' meadow, for birds she took for swans that were probably spur winged geese. She received the deed by 1688, and in 1695, by most accounts, the farm was sold to a burgher of the Russouw family, whose heirs held it for generations and built the gabled homestead. One historian has since questioned parts of that account, so the early years are told here as the house's story. The modern estate's white blend came with the 2007 vintage, when Steenberg released its first Magna Carta, Sauvignon Blanc with barrel fermented Sémillon. The house has made it only in years it judges strong enough, so none was released between 2017 and 2021. Magna Carta shows the ward's two signature white grapes at their most serious, and its name, the great charter, is the house's promise of quality.

records.table: Christine is Buitenverwachting's Bordeaux style red from the Constantiaberg slopes, Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc with Merlot, given two years in new French oak and years in bottle before release. It tastes of blackcurrant, cedar and tobacco, so decant it.
records.story: Buitenverwachting, beyond expectation, began as part of the Constantia estate granted to Simon van der Stel (1639 to 1712) in 1685. In 1773 it was first sold as a separate farm of two hundred morgen, and it changed hands many times after. By the house's account a member of the Cloete family of Groot Constantia took the farm in 1825 and planted some ninety thousand vines there that year, and from 1866 the farm's fortunes were bound to two Cape families, the Louws and the Lategans, joined by a marriage. In the twentieth century its vineyards fell into decline. In 1980 the farm was bought by a German industrial family, who restored the buildings, rebuilt the cellar and replanted the vineyards from the start; the first modern vintage followed in 1985, the first harvest the farm had seen in decades. Christine, a red blend in the Bordeaux manner named for a member of that family, became the house's flagship and was being made by the middle of the 1990s, only in years the house thought worthy. Christine is the wine to know for Constantia's reds: a cool ward famous for white wines, giving a firm, cedar scented Cabernet blend.

records.table: Five is Constantia Glen's flagship red, all five Bordeaux grapes from slopes below Constantia Nek, blended in shares that change with each vintage and aged in mostly new French oak. It shows cassis, cedar and graphite, so decant it young.
records.story: Constantia Glen lies at the head of the Constantia valley, just below the saddle of Constantia Nek between the Constantiaberg and Table Mountain. A family from Austria bought the farm, then called Glen Alpine, in 1960 by the house's account and built their homes there. For years it was not a vineyard at all: from 1995 to 2000 it ran a stud of Red Angus cattle. In January 2000 a wildfire swept the Cape Peninsula and cleared most of the farm's vegetation, and the family then commissioned soil tests across the property. The first vines went in that September, chosen for the Bordeaux grapes the slopes seemed to suit. The first white wine came in 2005 and the first reds in 2007, among them the blend of all five Bordeaux grapes that leads the range as Five. The house built its range on the number of grapes in each blend: Two for its white of Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon, Three for a red of three grapes, Five at the head. Five is the young face of Constantia: a farm of this century, far from the old sweet wine, making a Bordeaux style red on the ward's high, cool slopes.
